definition: A radar that finds aircraft by bouncing radio pulses off them. It needs no help from the aircraft, but it only sees a position.
The small part of a radar pulse that bounces off an object and comes back to the antenna.
How many pulses the radar sends every second. More pulses mean more hits on each aircraft but a shorter distance before echoes get mixed up.
The farthest distance an echo can come from and still arrive before the next pulse is sent. Beyond it, echoes are drawn at the wrong distance.
An echo from very far away that arrives after the next pulse has left, so the radar draws it much closer than it really is.
How wide the radar's beam is, in degrees. A narrow beam gives sharper direction and more range; a wide beam blurs nearby aircraft together.
How long the radar antenna takes to turn once. The screen gets a new position for each aircraft once per turn.
Unwanted echoes from the ground, buildings, rain, birds or wind farms that can hide real aircraft.
Echoes from hills, trees and buildings. They are strongest near the radar and on hillsides facing it.
Echoes from rain drops. Heavy rain shows up on a primary radar screen as a pale patch.
A filter that compares echoes from one pulse to the next and removes the ones that do not move, such as hills and buildings.
How fast something moves directly toward or away from the radar. An aircraft flying in a circle around the radar has no radial speed.
How big an object looks to a radar, in square metres. It depends on shape and material, not just size: a small aircraft is about 1 m², an airliner tens of m².
The rule that links transmitter power, antenna, target size and distance to the strength of the echo. The echo weakens with the fourth power of distance.
An early radar display that draws echo strength against time along one direction. Each bump is an echo; its time gives its distance.
The space directly above a radar where its beam does not reach, so aircraft overhead are not seen.
How close together in distance two aircraft can be before the radar sees them as one blip. Shorter pulses give finer resolution.
Radio frequencies around 2 to 4 GHz. Airport approach radars use about 2.7 to 2.9 GHz.
Radio frequencies around 1 to 2 GHz. Long-range en-route radars, SATCOM and GNSS use parts of this band.
How often a surveillance system gives a new position for each aircraft.
